subject: physics

moments.title: Maxwell formalises Faraday's field
moments.body:
Maxwell, in his late twenties, sets out to mathematise Faraday's lines of force. Over a decade he develops the field equations governing electric and magnetic phenomena. He adds a crucial new term — the displacement current — to make the equations self-consistent.

With the displacement current in, the equations have wave solutions.
moments.takeaway: Adding a missing term to make the equations consistent gives them wave solutions automatically.

moments.title: Maxwell predicts light is electromagnetic
moments.body:
Maxwell publishes 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field' in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society. The equations predict electromagnetic waves travel at speed c = 1 / √(μ0 ε0) — calculated from electric and magnetic constants measured in static lab experiments.

The result is exactly the measured speed of light. Maxwell concludes: 'We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.'

quote.text: We can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena.
quote.attrib: James Clerk Maxwell, A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field, 1865

moments.takeaway: Three sciences — electricity, magnetism, optics — collapse into one theory. Light is an electromagnetic wave.

moments.title: Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism
moments.body:
Maxwell publishes a two-volume treatise systematising the field. In the original notation it had 20 equations. Heaviside (in the 1880s) reformulates the system using modern vector calculus into the familiar four equations we now call 'Maxwell's equations'.

The four-equation form is what we teach today. Maxwell died young (cancer, 1879, age 48) and never saw his electromagnetic wave prediction experimentally confirmed.
moments.takeaway: The grand synthesis of 19th-century physics. Two volumes that defined the next century's electromagnetism.

moments.title: Hertz produces and detects radio waves
moments.body:
Hertz builds a spark-gap transmitter and a loop receiver. He generates electromagnetic waves at radio frequencies (about 30 MHz) and detects them across a room. He measures wavelength, polarisation and reflection — all consistent with Maxwell.

When asked about applications, Hertz says he sees none — 'It's of no use whatsoever... we just have these mysterious electromagnetic waves that we cannot see with the naked eye. But they are there.' Marconi will commercialise radio within 10 years.
moments.takeaway: Maxwell's prediction is experimentally confirmed in his absence. Radio waves are real.

now.title: Maxwell's equations today
now.body:
Maxwell's equations underpin radio, television, mobile phones, GPS, microwaves, lasers, MRI, the electricity grid and the entire optical-fibre internet backbone. They were one of the inputs to Einstein's special relativity (1905). Their relativistic completion is automatic.

Quantum electrodynamics (QED, Feynman, Schwinger, Tomonaga, Dyson — 1965 Nobel) extends Maxwell's equations to the quantum regime. QED is the most precisely tested theory in physics — the electron's magnetic moment is predicted and measured to about 12 decimal places.
now.open_questions: Can we generate and shape arbitrary quantum states of light? Are there modifications to QED at extreme energies or in extreme fields (e.g. photon-photon scattering observed at the LHC in 2017)? Could axion-like particles or a non-zero photon mass be detected in precision experiments?

reflection: Maxwell's equations predicted electromagnetic waves of all wavelengths but he only knew about light. Every part of the spectrum we now use (radio, microwaves, X-rays, gamma rays) was discovered after his death. How often does a theory predict more than its creators can imagine?
